title: Dates and times
summary: ISO text, date arithmetic, buckets by month and weekday, and how every database spells it differently.

steps.title: Dates in SQLite
body: The final month. Rosa hands you the problems every real database has: dates, messy text, JSON, duplicates. First, Inkwell & Ivy's new **web shop**.
SQLite has no date type. Dates are stored as **ISO-8601 text** (`'2026-09-03 09:15:00'`), which sorts and compares correctly as text, and a few functions understand it:
```sql
SELECT strftime('%w', '2026-09-03');                 -- 4 (0 = Sunday)
SELECT date('2026-09-03', 'start of month', '+1 month', '-1 day');  -- 2026-09-30
SELECT julianday('2026-09-07') - julianday('2026-09-03');           -- 4.0 (days)
`'now'` gives the current time (`date('now')`), which makes results change every day: great in apps, useless in tests.

code: SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', placed_at) AS month, COUNT(*)
setup: CREATE TABLE web_orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer TEXT NOT NULL, placed_at TEXT NOT NULL, shipped_at TEXT, total_cents INTEGER NOT NULL);
steps.explain: `strftime('%Y-%m', ...)` buckets each order into its month.

steps.title: Revenue by month
prompt: Return **month** (`YYYY-MM`) and **revenue** (sum of total_cents) per month, in order.
Tables: `web_orders(id, customer, placed_at, shipped_at, total_cents)`; times are ISO text like `'2026-09-03 09:15:00'`; `shipped_at` is NULL until shipped.
solution: SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', placed_at) AS month, SUM(total_cents) AS revenue
setup: CREATE TABLE web_orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer TEXT NOT NULL, placed_at TEXT NOT NULL, shipped_at TEXT, total_cents INTEGER NOT NULL);

steps.prompt: Match each expression to its result.

steps.title: Shipping speed
prompt: For every **shipped** order return **id**, **customer** and **days_to_ship**: the time from placed to shipped in days, rounded to 1 decimal. Slowest first; ties broken by id.
Tables: `web_orders(id, customer, placed_at, shipped_at, total_cents)`; times are ISO text like `'2026-09-03 09:15:00'`; `shipped_at` is NULL until shipped.
solution: SELECT id, customer, ROUND(julianday(shipped_at) - julianday(placed_at), 1) AS days_to_ship
setup: CREATE TABLE web_orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer TEXT NOT NULL, placed_at TEXT NOT NULL, shipped_at TEXT, total_cents INTEGER NOT NULL);
hints: `julianday(b) - julianday(a)` is the difference in days, with fractions.
Leave out unshipped orders: `shipped_at IS NOT NULL`.

steps.title: Every database, its own date functions
body: Date handling is where dialects differ most. A cheat sheet:
```text
task              SQLite                          PostgreSQL                   SQL Server                      MySQL
now               datetime('now')                 now()                        SYSDATETIME()                   NOW()
today             date('now')                     CURRENT_DATE                 CAST(GETDATE() AS date)         CURDATE()
add 7 days        date(d, '+7 days')              d + INTERVAL '7 days'        DATEADD(day, 7, d)              DATE_ADD(d, INTERVAL 7 DAY)
days between      julianday(b) - julianday(a)     b::date - a::date            DATEDIFF(day, a, b)             DATEDIFF(b, a)
month bucket      strftime('%Y-%m', d)            date_trunc('month', d)       DATETRUNC(month, d) (2022+)     DATE_FORMAT(d, '%Y-%m')
year              strftime('%Y', d)               EXTRACT(YEAR FROM d)         YEAR(d)                         YEAR(d)
Two habits that work everywhere: store timestamps in **UTC**, and filter ranges as `>= start AND < next_start` (SARGable, and correct for the last second of the day).

steps.prompt: Which filter correctly selects every order placed in **October 2026** and can use an index on `placed_at`?
steps.explain: BETWEEN stops at `'2026-10-31'`, which sorts **before** `'2026-10-31 23:50:00'`, so Chloe's late-night order is lost. The strftime version also matches October of every year and can't use an index.

steps.title: Still waiting
prompt: Customer care wants unshipped orders and how long they've waited **as of 2026-11-05 12:00:00** (use that fixed time, not `'now'`). Return **id**, **customer** and **days_waiting** rounded to 1 decimal.
Tables: `web_orders(id, customer, placed_at, shipped_at, total_cents)`; times are ISO text like `'2026-09-03 09:15:00'`; `shipped_at` is NULL until shipped.
solution: SELECT id, customer, ROUND(julianday('2026-11-05 12:00:00') - julianday(placed_at), 1) AS days_waiting
setup: CREATE TABLE web_orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer TEXT NOT NULL, placed_at TEXT NOT NULL, shipped_at TEXT, total_cents INTEGER NOT NULL);

steps.title: Weekend orders
prompt: Return the number of orders placed on each **day of the week**: **weekday** (`Sun`, `Mon`, ... `Sat`) and **orders**. Only days with orders.
Tables: `web_orders(id, customer, placed_at, shipped_at, total_cents)`; times are ISO text like `'2026-09-03 09:15:00'`; `shipped_at` is NULL until shipped.
solution: WHEN '0' THEN 'Sun' WHEN '1' THEN 'Mon' WHEN '2' THEN 'Tue' WHEN '3' THEN 'Wed'
WHEN '4' THEN 'Thu' WHEN '5' THEN 'Fri' ELSE 'Sat' END AS weekday,
setup: CREATE TABLE web_orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer TEXT NOT NULL, placed_at TEXT NOT NULL, shipped_at TEXT, total_cents INTEGER NOT NULL);
hints: A CASE turns the digit into a name; GROUP BY the CASE's alias.
